speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore's education system is said by many to be one of the best in the world.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, we are not perfect and we face our own giants.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At a recent Meet-the-People session, a couple with three children asked me to appeal for more childcare subsidies for her younger ones.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is still thriving as a shadow education industry.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) cut-off points for entry into secondary schools of one's choice are a key performance indicator (KPI) for not only many students, but also their parents and school educators.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some educators feel that the education rat race has begun even before one enters Primary 1.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Others fear that meritocracy is at risk of losing its place as a social leveller as those in the higher-income groups self-perpetuate themselves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Woe be the day when a child's postal code determines his destiny.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Then, for those who learn differently, whether in special or mainstream schools, including the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs), quality of support is still inconsistent.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Education excellence for this group of learners is still an aspiration.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As a member of the Government Parliamentary Committee for Education for many years, I know that the Ministry has been diligently confronting these mountains.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They and many other Singaporeans know we must level the playing field so that every child has the opportunity to excel.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In January this year, I had spoken at length about the unhealthy trends of our preoccupation with academic success; "parentocracy" and the physical segregation of students based on their learning abilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I had also given several suggestions, including removing the high-stakes PSLE at the age of 12, but retaining the rigour of academic learning; and a review of the current model of sorting students into geographically different physical schools which may not reflect the microcosm of society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, use technology to empower students, families and educators to access the best education practices and resources in content, pedagogy and assessment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Three, review the PSLE, the Gifted Education Programme (GEP) and DSA systems and reduce the obsession with academic scores and perceived "elite" schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And four, provide better support to those with special needs in special schools and mainstream schools, including IHLs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, I want to touch upon future-proofing the education industry.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Our education sector is not immune to the fast-changing world that Budget 2016 has warned us about.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The need to fend off disruptive advances, move from value-adding to value-creation, getting into the Internet of Things are, I believe, as real in the not-for-profit education landscape as it is in the business sector.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Surely, there is a similar need for the Ministry of Education (MOE), like the rest of Singapore's key industries, to develop an industry future-proof transformation plan to look into deepening innovation capabilities and to help our people adjust and seize new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SkillsFuture was the first salvo to future-proof our nation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It represents a strategic and new look at how Singapore looks at schooling and learning – instead of a paper chase – and skills mastery, lifelong and self-driven learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How about learners who continue to learn long after their traditional school exit at the age of 18 or 21?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How can the current schools, including special schools and IHLs, be relevant to all of them?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Besides doing things to our students, we should work with partners to develop an Education Sectoral Manpower Plan.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Resources ought to be invested heavily in developing the future-ready mindsets and skillsets of educators and parents.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, to future-proof our education sector, I feel there is the need to speed up the application of technology to bring excellence to many more.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Besides its plan to launch an online learning space for its students, can MOE build an open-source platform to allow participants to develop, evaluate and contribute education ware?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Page: 8 Some of us have heard of The Independent Project where United States (US) high school students are allowed to start a mini school for themselves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Across the world, there are dream-school projects which are collaborations with researchers and innovative businesses, born out of a need for more effective and future-ready models for content, delivery and assessment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: MOE should give space to develop dream-school projects that can address current hot buttons and further future-proof ourselves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Lastly, on education for a caring and resilient society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I commend MOE’s recent plans to have all students clean up their school on a daily basis.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I also support its plan to build resilience in our youths through its National Outdoor Adventure Education Masterplan.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The goal of an excellent education must be the character of a person and must be based on a few key principles.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Students gather their morals and values from their experiences.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, that seeing is believing; and the modelling of the significant adults in a student's life is worth many lectures on good character.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As Ralph Waldo Emerson puts it, "Your actions speak so loudly I cannot hear what you are saying".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Three, that serving others must be the rent one pays for being here on earth, and to whom much is given, much is also expected.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are so many ways by which the education sector can contribute to the making of a caring and resilient society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Ad hoc or piecemeal efforts bear little impact either for the giver or the receiver.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One of the ways is to adopt a targeted approach to adopt causes on a committed basis and serve those who need a leg up.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Page: 9 Antoine de Saint-Exupery, the author of the classic "The Little Prince", was believed to have said, "If you want to build a ship, don't herd people together to collect wood and assign them tasks and work, but rather teach them first to yearn for the endless immensity of the sea." I look forward to both yearning for the sea and building a ship with the Ministry and my fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are now promulgating multiple pathways to diverse peaks of excellence in our education system.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In our bid to make our education system more diverse and holistic, we have to include more co-curricular activities (CCAs), outdoor learning, the creative arts and community involvement in our school curriculum.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I laud the move to recognise students' involvement in clubs, societies, sports, music and drama as part of the formal school curriculum, hence, placing such involvement as CCAs, rather than what was previously known as extracurricular activities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is good because values, such as resilience, sportsmanship, having the spirit of teamwork and developing one's leadership skills, can be honed.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, currently, students' involvement in CCAs depends a lot on their ability in a particular interest group.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, before a student is able to join the school's netball or football team, the student has to undergo trials to see if they are good enough to be part of the school team.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The purpose of CCAs is to allow more of our students to have a more balanced and holistic education in schools.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, the integration of outdoor learning and creative arts in our main school curriculum will strengthen learning and personal development of our students in schools.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Schools in countries, such as Finland, have incorporated outdoor learning in their curriculum where students learn map reading and trekking and put the knowledge learnt in Mathematics, Geography and Physics into practice; while schools in Australia have incorporated creative arts in their curriculum where students learn to appreciate music, visual arts, drama and dance and apply the knowledge learnt in English, Literature and Physical Education.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would even propose that appreciation of music, dance and culture of the different ethnicities in Singapore be included in our creative arts curriculum.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Being involved in the community through projects and outreach programmes helps foster values, such as empathy, caring for others and magnanimity.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Ministry will continue to build on our Values in Action programme and grant sufficient space for our students to design and implement their own community outreach projects so that they are able to learn and internalise these values in a more authentic manner.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Page: 10 On inclusivity, the new PSLE scoring system that was first announced by the Prime Minister at the National Day Rally in 2013 is a strong signal to parents, teachers and students of our move away from chasing the last point for the PSLE aggregate score.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This chase, in turn, affects admission to secondary schools, particularly those that are more popular than others and where the school cut-off points can be rather high.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a result of such keen competition to gain admission to these popular schools, many students depend on the DSA to leverage their other talents, such as in sports, music, dance or specific academic subjects.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are students who may not have met these popular schools' cut-off points for PSLE but have talents in other areas.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There have been some concerns that popular schools which admit students through DSA in non-academic areas may end up having these students under-performing or doing poorly in national examinations, hence, affecting the schools' overall performance.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I can understand that some popular schools are proud of their traditions and would like to retain a certain standard of excellence among their students.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, excellence cannot just mean achievement in academics.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Excellence must be holistic and include those in sports, the arts, music and community work and volunteerism.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The diversity in student population created would then be more representative of the larger community where different abilities exist and where the environment is not so exclusive.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As schools strive to create greater diversity among students and provide multiple pathways of excellence for them to pursue their interests and abilities in, there must also be efforts to ensure that our schools are a lot more inclusive.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are Allied Educators for Learning and Page: 11 Behavioural Support, or AED(LBS), who can help students with special needs in the classroom.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I envision our schools to be a lot more inclusive, being a microcosm of our society, where various abilities and disabilities exist together, and where our students learn to work together and help one another with compassion and magnanimity.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Even the DSA exercise has just been an entry route for students who have had the resources or opportunity to be developed in certain areas of sports or arts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At the end of the day, children are still pushed to compete against others, if not in academics, then in sports or arts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Competition is a fact of life, and we do our children a disservice if we do not prepare them for it.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But we also need them to appreciate that human beings cannot be measured like the weight of fish or the height of trees.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And our children need to develop in a less stressful and competitive way.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is an encouraging development, but how will this be aligned with the review of the PSLE system?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Will school admissions still be based on how well the children perform academically or in that area of specialisation or more based on whether the child's interest and aptitude match the school's programme?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister tell us how we can carry this through to primary school so that it is not necessary to just "cram" at the PSLE level and make it a must to get into that one good school?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: However, if MOE were to divide the 2015 cohort size by the number of secondary schools, it can easily fill all schools, including these seven schools, with at least five to six classes of 40 students each.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Thus, the reality is that all schools are created not equal, as popular schools will continue to attract more students at the expense of neighbourhood schools.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These call into question the mantra that every Page: 12 school is a good school.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The mad rush to become a parent volunteer, join the Residents’ Committee or even relocate just to secure a better chance in the balloting exercise for admission into popular schools for their children has become a stressful ritual for parents year after year.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, in the minds of parents, every school is definitely not the same.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am sure when teachers and principals come together, the issue of funding for their schools will surface somewhere down their conversation.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is my belief that MOE must walk the talk that every school is, indeed a good school by addressing the funding issues first.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In a reply to my Parliamentary Question on funding for schools, the Minister said it is not meaningful to compare funding per school but rather we should look at the per capita funding per student.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, while we know that every student can be a good student because they are given the same per capita funding, I am not sure if every school can be a good school in the context of funding at the school level.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Popular schools with higher enrolment numbers, by default, will have more budget to work with.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This, in my opinion, creates an unlevel playing field for less popular schools.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I shall confine my speech to primary education to illustrate this point.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Let us compare Rosyth Primary School with an enrolment of 2,000 students with Bendemeer Primary School with an enrolment of 1,200 students.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This disparity will perpetuate year after year as popular schools with bigger budgets will be able to do more for their students, and at a lower cost due to economies of scale.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And when schools churn out even more top students, it will be a hard sell to tell parents that every school is a good school because neighbourhood schools will be shrinking in size and disappearing over time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We do not need the mainstream media to publicise anything anymore.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The popular schools will get more popular through the grapevine.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Does the Minister not agree that it makes a world of difference for principals and teachers of smaller neighbourhood schools to have a comparable amount of funding as those popular schools to run their programmes each year?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For a less popular school with a smaller cohort, the extra funding will come in handy to compensate for the lower economies of scale in the procurement of products and services for their students.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Currently, primary schools are already recognising their top PSLE students.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, the chances Page: 13 of top students from neighbourhood primary schools going to popular schools like Dunman High, Hwa Chong or Raffles Institution are no lesser than their peers from popular primary schools now and still based on merit at the school level.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This will ensure a good mix and spread of students from all spectrum of primary school going into secondary school.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This will also prevent elitism from entrenching itself in the feeding primary school and the popular secondary school.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This new posting exercise will make every primary school a good school, as the top graduating student in each school will have a direct entry to a school of their choice.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For parents who want their children to attend a popular secondary school, every primary school is a good school to start the journey now.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Equitable funding means levelling the playing field for neighbourhood schools so that they will have additional funds to invest in varied arts, sports and enrichment programmes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will help develop students more holistically and improve the overall quality of schools.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Ministry has a long-standing position that schools are resourced on a needs-basis, depending on programmes offered and the enrolment of the school.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, if a neighbourhood school has lesser funding to begin with, how can the school even start to invest in, say, a niche elective in the first place to justify for additional funding?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, neighbourhood schools do not enjoy the privileges of independent schools like higher school fees and a wealthy alumni.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How does the Ministry take this into account in schools' funding criteria to ensure fairness?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we see more schools merge due to lower enrolment, it is a good opportunity for the Ministry to redistribute funding across neighbourhood schools to equalise this disparity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yes, resources may only be a part of the solution, but it is, nonetheless a basic and critical component.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe that equitable funding is a realistic and worthwhile objective that the Ministry should seriously consider.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These schemes and the relevant awards are significant in motivating students who display excellence and commitment during the course of Page: 14 their educational endeavours.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Members of this House would be familiar with some of these schemes.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These include the Financial Assistance Scheme, EduSave scheme and the Opportunity Fund scheme.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In their respective ways, these schemes go a long way in helping and supporting needy students in their educational, enrichment and personal pursuits.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is in this spirit of lending a helping hand to our children and fostering their respective development, where every child is an invaluable asset to the future of this country, that we should further assess the feasibility of extending all MOE assistance schemes, awards and funds to all eligible Singaporean students, including those who are receiving their education in private institutions.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As a Ministry that is tasked to nurture the holistic development of every precious Singaporean son and daughter, the extension of its schemes to all eligible Singaporean students, regardless of their choice of school, is a bold act of inclusivity that will motivate our children to aim for the horizon and pursue the rainbow before them.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Let us partner our children and lead them down the many unknowns in their educational life with anticipation, hope and joy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We communicate our intentions in three ways: through what we say, what we do and what we reward.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And each form of communication is more important than the last, and people always listen to rewards the most.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: No matter what you say, they will take what you reward as the truth of what you really want.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, if we care about priming our kids in the habits needed for innovation and collaboration later, we have to build in the reward of those behaviours into the school system now.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I was wondering if MOE could consider collaborating with researchers and just one or two progressive primary schools to prototype a solution trying out these two interventions.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: MOE has eight stated outcomes of what a kid should have achieved by Primary 6, including great things like: one, they know their strengths; two, they have a lively curiosity about things; and three, they cooperate, share and care for others.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But because every primary school still dedicates the biggest real estate on report cards to subject grades, every stakeholder gets the message that these outcomes do not really matter.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If these behaviours are not tracked or rewarded on a report card, it is not going to happen systematically; just accidentally.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: You can hear few parents freaking out about their child not "knowing their strengths" or stressing about Ah-Boy's lack of "curiosity", even though that is actually more indicative of future success.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I suggest we give significant space on report cards to non-academic indicators closely linked to our strategic outcomes of innovation and collaboration.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Principals can collaborate with researchers and staff to develop a policy that grounds everyone in a common Page: 15 agreement on what productive, purposeful homework looks.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Homework also comes with clearly marked learning objectives to prevent miscommunication.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A succinct and specific set of standards less than a page long makes clear to all stakeholders from the start what to expect from the school in terms of ideology, quantity and quality of assignments.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, a school that believes in family-friendly homework policy could say something upfront like, "In here, our Primary 1s get three traditional academic assignments and two unconventional homework assignments that have academic and non-academic purposes".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Differentiated homework policies can help schools build up distinctive cultures appealing to distinctive types of parents.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I hope MOE can consider piloting a Mindful School strategy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are important but in the 21st century, we will increasingly need qualities like leadership, initiative, confidence, creativity, communication skills and altruism.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we have stopped publishing PSLE top scorers and the like, I fear credentialism is still deeply entrenched among parents, teachers and students, and we need to break this self-reinforcing loop.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, in Singapore, parent-teacher meetings (PTMs) often take the form of the teacher explaining the gaps in the child's performance without the child being present, with the view to the parent helping to remedy those gaps at home.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do not blame our teachers at all for this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are doing their jobs as defined by the system, and usually they are motivated by genuine care for their children.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But contrast this with the PTM held at one western international school here that I learned about.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PTM was run by the children themselves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are a number of international measures of such qualities that could be surveyed each year without recourse to mass standardised testing and which warrant further study by MOE.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Initiating one's project, like setting up a new club, a new sports activity, a charitable project, an informal business activity and so on, both reflects and nurtures just the kind of qualities that we need in the 21st century.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: We believe CCAs inculcate values, such as perseverance, and help students develop transferable skills in organising, planning, self-discipline and other areas.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: There are stories of students turned away from certain CCAs because the students have no reasonable prospects of winning trophies for lack of prior training or natural ability.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In fact, it appears that the further students progress in their education, the more difficult they find it to participate in CCAs and sports or in the performing arts.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: CCA participation, I feel, should importantly be based on students' keen interest to take part, in addition to their demonstrated competency.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Allowing students to follow their interest will keep them motivated to remain in the CCAs for the long term and reap the rich educational benefits that CCAs in schools have to offer.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, you have two cuts, please take them together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will be modelled after the US' "Teach for America" and the UK's "Teach First Programmes", both of which have good track records in improving educational outcomes for underprivileged students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should, of course, make specific adaptations to the Singapore context.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The aim is to create a national core of dedicated alumni who will continue to inspire and improve one another through conferences, courses and retreats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will seed and grow the pursuit for education and equality and social mobility among our teachers as well as close the school quality gap.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Only in GEP are class sizes kept at 25 to promote better teacher-student engagement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand that the pupil-teacher ratios for primary and secondary schools are equivalent to OECD averages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But teachers in Singapore are deployed to provide support and extra classes for low-progress students rather than to reduce class sizes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, reducing class sizes will remove the need to provide these extra remedial classes, which reinforce the stressful tuition culture in schools.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nothing beats the close attention paid to students by the primary teacher in class and only a smaller class size can facilitate this.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: I must say we are making some progress, albeit not to the level of civic consciousness like in Japan or Switzerland.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: We all know we need to cultivate a mindset of civic consciousness and we need to start young.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: We all know that but, for some reason, these mindsets get reset rather easily each time we are out in the public.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: We are taught to clear our own trays from preschool to university, in the army camp and at home, and yet we have so much problem doing that in our hawker centre, food court and even in this Parliament, Madam.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: I always wonder what is impeding our effort to become a gracious society after 50 years of nationhood.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Perhaps, we need to refocus, reset and redouble our effort to achieve that in the next chapter of our history.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Last year, I urged the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources to bring back the spirit of the Keep Singapore Clean campaign.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: This Committee of Supply (COS), I would like to urge MOE to plant the seeds of civic consciousness into our young again.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: We not only need to teach our young about ownership and responsibility, we also need to make them appreciate how hard our cleaners are working every day, and that keeping Singapore clean is not just the job of the cleaners but everyone else's responsibility as well.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: It has to begin at home and in the school.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: We have to constantly work to get the mindset right in our young, so that they will lend themselves readily to acts of kindness, volunteer work and philanthropy for the betterment of society when they grow up.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: While I urge parents to do their part at home, I urge our schools to teach our children well, so that, together, we can make civic consciousness a way of life.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In my encounters working as an educator with children, youths and adults, many have been scarred by deep-seated emotional issues, such as loss, for example, when a child has to part with a long-familiar domestic helper at the end of her contract or when a pet dies or when a child's precious toy is thrown away without his or her knowledge or consent.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There are also cases of more extreme losses and adjustments for the young: when they leave their friends in school and move on; when family members pass away; when their school or classmates die suddenly in accidents or even suicides.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It pains us greatly, as adults, to see young people struggle in such circumstances.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What we cannot prevent, we should prevail, we should overcome.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The pain and burden of a child in school should be carried by more than just the child.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: A caring society should begin with a humane school environment, one that places value on compassion as much as competition, and goodwill as much as grades.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Emotional upheavals should not be dismissed as personal failure, as if those who go through pain somehow deserve it because they had not done enough to prevent it.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Shanmugam shared about the difficulty of getting whole families to participate in the rehabilitative process when they face problems.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Imagine how many more unknown problems exist out there, with families unwilling to speak of their pain, let alone seek help.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In this context, I would like to advocate for schools to take on a proactive role in preparing young people to deal with emotional distress.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: My predecessor, Nominated Member of Parliament for the arts, Ms Janice Koh, had spoken passionately about the importance of literature.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Led by facilitators with strategies, reading sessions can help students access the lives of characters and understand their deeper emotions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In this way, the students can better deal with similar issues that they may be facing.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: For primary school students, we can use relatable stories, like taking care of pets, to examine issues of loss.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: For higher levels, we can tackle more complex situations.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Students have to be guided in the process.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And I would think that experiential learning would be a good strategy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Experiential learning builds within the body a memory that does not forget easily and help the students to cope.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: You cannot intellectually learn how to ride a bicycle; you have to go on it, fall.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But after a while, you realise that even if you do not ride a bicycle, you will still remember how to do it because your body recalls it for you.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To deal with the issues in the classroom may sound very daunting.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But these operations often appear to be detached from the daily grind of school life – as if being in touch with a counsellor is a sign of weakness or, worse, a taboo.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Imagine then if such teacher-counsellors are part and parcel of school life.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Imagine if a child can ask questions about algebra and fractions in one class, and then talk about the pain of losing her favourite cat minutes later.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that a multi-agency approach is required to effect this change in our social, familial and education systems.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Some may think that my proposals would mean that parents are excused from their responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I would, however, like to suggest a paradigm shift: let us begin work on the young, so that as they grow in their ability to handle change and loss, they, in turn, can be the living examples that their children can learn from.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Would this not be groundbreaking, effective and empowering?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As I speak, I remember this young adolescent whom I taught, who cuts himself to stop his girlfriend from cutting herself also.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The best story was his mother left home when he was very young.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: His father never explained to him why he had to go through this.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: He is living through the pain and, now, he does not want his girlfriend to go.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The philosopher Arthur Schopenhaur said: mostly, it is loss which teaches us the worth of things.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: While they are tech-savvy, they may or may not be Internet-savvy.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They are comfortable navigating the Internet and may forget there are real dangers lurking in cyberspace which they have to guard and protect themselves against.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Cyberbullying, online predators and online scams are just some of the dangers that youths face.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some people believe that it is the parents' duty to protect their children from online threats.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: While this may be true, it is difficult for parents to monitor and control the online behaviour of their children.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Parents are often less tech-savvy than their children.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We have to equip our children and youths with the skills to navigate the Internet safely and to differentiate between fact and fiction, outdated news and incorrect sources.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, it is a well-known fact that students learn and develop at different rates and different pace at different periods of their lives.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Some are fast learners during the early years and plateau as they grow older while some are late bloomers.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: MOE has set the noble mission of inculcating learning for mastery, learning throughout life and learning for life.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In our very fast-paced formal education system, how does the proposed learning for mastery fit in?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: For some students who may need more time to master their subjects, they will lag behind their peers if insufficient time is given to achieve mastery.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They may pass the tests and exams with just above 50 marks and get promoted to next level.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: When they reach the next level, the difficulty level of the subject is going to be raised another notch.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Since they did not have a chance to master the subject, their weak foundation will give way and they may lose interest in learning the subject.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am concerned with under-performing students, in particular, those from low-income families.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Not every home is able to offer a conducive environment to study, especially for those in rental flats where space is limited and those from dysfunctional families.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Poverty becomes a vicious cycle and social mobility is hindered.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Some students fall into bad company when they get discouraged by their poor performance and there is no one at home to supervise them.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There are teachers who would stay back after school on their own accord and at their own expense.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Nevertheless, we cannot expect every teacher to do so, because of the heavy workload.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I hope that there is more assistance from the self-help groups which offer student care services at subsidised rates.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They are planning to join hands to run as many as 30 centres.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am concerned whether they have enough resources.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Does the Ministry have any plan to support them?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What is the Ministry doing to track these weaker students and their progress and give them more support?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What is being done to help those whose parents cannot afford tuition?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Is there an early warning system so that the Ministry can intervene when a weak student is spotted?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: Research has also shown that eating habits and food preferences are acquired when young and are more difficult to change after adolescence.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: I hope these will enable the Ministry and HPB to further cut down the amount of sugar allowed in the food and drinks sold in our schools, be they juice, carbonated, or other types of drinks, for the further Page: 21 promotion of health among our school children.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many schools now realise that the job of educating students cannot be achieved by their efforts alone.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Rather, it requires a collaborative effort with families, communities and other stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In most of our schools, there is some measure of parent and community involvement and it is usually directed and guided by the schools, with the main focus being on fundraising initiatives, volunteering and supporting school activities.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, moving forward, I feel community partnership should go beyond such traditional engagement and be expanded to involve families and the broader community in decision-making and school governance.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When schools actively involve parents and engage community resources, they are able to respond more effectively to the learning needs and create an environment conducive to the general well-being of the students.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: To do so, they should not have to wake up very early in the morning and then make their way to school which may be 30-45 minutes away from home.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Several other factors are considered like whether a sibling is at the same school, whether the parent is a former student or alumni from that school or whether the parents are linked to the school through a religious order, clan association or community leader.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I acknowledge the importance of each factor in wanting schools to have links to former students and to develop a school culture.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, whatever reason a parent has for wanting a child to attend a particular primary school, it simply does not make sense for young six- or seven-year-old students to have to travel more than 20 minutes to attend their school.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This way, the students benefit from having more time to sleep and not having to wake up at some unearthly hour.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: The Compulsory Education Act implemented since 2003 has been instrumental in ensuring that our children have at least six years of primary education.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Although Page: 22 the Act is in force and there are penalties under the Act to act as a deterrent, the responsibility of sending children to school for primary education and ensuring they remain in school during those six years still remains with the parents.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: I support compulsory education as I believe our children need a solid educational foundation that is not just about gaining knowledge, but also includes social interaction and developing communication skills.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: However, I would like to propose that the Ministry consider extending compulsory education even earlier, to the preschool level.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Substantial research has shown that a child's learning ability is at its peak between the ages of two and five years.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Their language ability increases manifold, moving from knowing about 50 words at the age of two, to at least 1,000 words by the age of five, when they learn to think, reason, read, count and identity colours, their body parts, the planets, the solar system, the different dinosaurs and just about every other category of objects.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: They also develop their social and emotional intelligence during these crucial years and, by age five, they would have learnt how to make friends and remember their friends' names and birthdays.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: For this group of children, they start Primary 1 without much preschool preparation and with what, I believe, to be insufficient optimum cognitive and socio-emotional development.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: MOE has already embarked on providing preschool education and has established MOE Kindergartens which now number about 15 centres around the island.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Accessibility and affordability to preschool education would not be a prohibitive factor for parents not to send their children to preschool.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: The intent is not to make it difficult for parents or to enforce the Compulsory Education Act on them.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: The intent is really to ensure that our children have an earlier start at developing cognitive, social and communication skills, and to give a boost to children from less privileged families to help them have a better start at primary school.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: It would also encourage others to start a family in the near future as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Nevertheless, parents in Singapore are rightfully very concerned about education opportunities for their children.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Accessibility and affordability of related services, preschool education in particular, are the concerns of parents.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I have spoken, like many other Members in this House, on the importance of early childhood education on the overall development of our children and have appealed to the Government to put in more resources to enhance early childhood education as it is an important social leveller.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I have Page: 23 also proposed that the Government build larger early childhood education centres similar to our primary schools instead of tucking them at void decks.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Will MOE consider starting mega early childhood centres or kindergartens so that there are economies of scale and better career prospects for our early childhood educators?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can MOE consider using the premises of soon-to-be closed secondary schools to run this project?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: In the past years, the Government has done quite a lot to enhance the quality of early childhood education, keep fees affordable and increase the number of early childhood education centres in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Early childhood educators are getting more relevant training as well as employment perks.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: But to create a children-friendly society that embraces the concept of families, we have to do more to enhance the quality of the centres that we have in Singapore now.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: How adequate is the current supply of early childhood education centres in matching the demand?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What are the plans in place to expand this network of early childhood education?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We should consider investing in the training of early childhood educators and the pedagogy of doing so.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We are dealing with the foundation years which are very important to our students.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: How aware and well-prepared are our early childhood educators in identifying these problems to facilitate early diagnosis and intervention?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Many families have both parents who are working.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: They usually put their children in a full-day childcare centre or kindergarten.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: When the child enrols in a primary school, after-school care services are critical for this group.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: There seems to be a mismatch between full-day childcare and after-school care services.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can the Government do a more accurate projection of the demand for after-school care services in each estate by the number of children who are in full-day childcare?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Most parents prefer to put their children in after-school care services in the same primary school.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Since all primary schools are going single session, can the Ministry put an after-school care service in all primary schools and cater to all students who need it?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can the Minister update the House on the status of this programme?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: When can we see all our 190 primary schools having their student care centres?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I hope MOE can ramp up the number of student care centres faster to cater for the demand to match MSF's rate of ramping up childcare centres.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I think I have forgotten Mr Zainal Sapari.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Compared to private preschool education, MOE has more resources to develop a comprehensive preschool curriculum.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I would like MOE to provide an update on programmes and resources that will be made available to more pre-school centres to support them in building this strong foundation.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Will MOE develop a framework to share the expertise with private school operators?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Such a framework to support private-school operators will level up standards to ensure quality preschool education will be accessible to all, just like general education in all our mainstream schools.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: It is my dream that any child can get the best quality preschool education, regardless of the fees that the parents are paying.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Chia, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Could the Minister let us know: (a) the number of students who have received assistance from DSOs to date and the nature and outcome of such assistance; (b) the number of students who have utilised the SEN fund and the average amount utilised; (c) whether the Ministry is satisfied with the take-up rate; and (d) what measures would the Ministry be taking to facilitate students taking up more of such services?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Page: 25 Currently, all primary schools are staffed with at least one AED(LBS) to support students with mild special educational needs (SENs).

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: MOE is continuing to train teachers in special needs, and I thank the Ministry for that.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: The current training, unfortunately, is undertaken by individual schools on a request basis where special potential training providers submit training proposals.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Can I suggest that the Ministry consider, specifically approaching training providers for more efficiency and greater efficacy in outcome?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Hence, parents with special needs children would prefer their children to be in specialised schools where there is better support, but either there are no vacancies in those schools or the cost of putting their child in these specialised schools is too expensive as they may not be eligible for subsidies.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I would like MOE to consider improving the ratio of SNOs to the number of special needs children in schools.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: MOE should also consider having more special needs schools and providing more support for special needs children.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Ideally, the school fees must be the same as those paid by students in mainstream schools.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Every parent wants the best for their child and I believe there is something that we can do as the Government to show that, indeed, we care for every Singaporean student.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: All of us value education, as individuals and also as a society.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For individual students and families, it is a journey of hopes and aspirations, as well as anxieties.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For the country, education is a strategic pillar of nation-building and economic and social development.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is important to take both perspectives as we evolve our education system with the changing times.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is a significant shift for MOE, together with all our stakeholders.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It will involve not just the schools, but also our IHLs, parents and our industry and community partners.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Page: 26 Minister Ong Ye Kung and I will talk about this shift today.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Many Members have spoken about global developments as well as changes in the local operating environment, such as our ageing population and shrinking workforce.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These will impact Singapore, our security and economy.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: With changes, there will also be new opportunities, such as the growth of frontier markets and disruptive innovations like robotics, 3D printing and the Internet of Things.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Committee on the Future Economy (CFE) is looking at how Singapore can reframe the way we add value to the world and enable our people to be future-ready.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MOE supports this effort closely in our schools and IHLs.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our education system must prepare our future generations to embrace this increasingly complex and dynamic world and preserve and strengthen the cohesiveness of our society.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This goes beyond providing our children with academic knowledge.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It includes helping them to learn the right values and attitudes, and the broader attributes and competencies to navigate the demands of life and work.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They will need to be adaptable and resilient to face uncertainties and change.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Just as important, they must grow up with a heart for Singapore and fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Hence, the education that we gift our children should be holistic.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Every child should be provided with opportunities to discover and develop his or her strengths and interests in multiple domains.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Every child should grow up a well-rounded individual, a lifelong learner who pursues mastery and fulfilment in a domain of his or her choice.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I believe that this is the best way forward to prepare our young people and nation for the future.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: To prepare our children for the future, we need a collective paradigm shift.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Today, academic excellence is a hallmark of the Singapore education system.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our students rank highly in international benchmarking studies.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are recognised for the high standards that we have achieved.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, the focus of our education system should go beyond test scores.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is deeply ingrained in our culture, translated into the expectations of our children, parents and teachers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Eventually, this is perhaps even manifested in the employers’ mindsets at workplaces.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We need to free up time and space to nurture other dimensions that are just as important for our children's development.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Let them not just study the flowers, but also stop to smell the flowers and wonder at their beauty.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We want to cultivate a generation of young people who grow up with a sense of curiosity and a love for learning, asking both the "whys" and, sometimes, even the "why-nots".

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But this would not be an easy or straightforward thing to do.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As we often say, in education, it takes a village to raise a child, but that also means it takes the whole village to change the way we raise a child.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MOE and our fraternity of educators have taken the lead and made improvements to policies, structures and processes over time.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Page: 27 But policy changes can only go so far.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is not something that MOE can do unilaterally or from the top down.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We need a partnership with parents and the community to make this shift, and this will take time.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Students, parents, educators and employers must come on board and adjust mindsets and behaviours as well, together with MOE.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Schools leverage curricular and co-curricular programmes to design meaningful learning opportunities and provide students with regular feedback to help them develop in these non-academic aspects.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For example, subjects, such as design and technology and project work, provide avenues for students to develop creativity and innovation.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Students also get opportunities to develop and apply leadership, initiative and collaboration through Values-in-Action (VIA) projects and CCAs.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I am glad to share that our schools regularly review the progress of our students and the effectiveness of all programmes in developing our students holistically, not just in their academics.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ms Kuik spoke about redesigning student report cards to reflect non-academic attributes.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Parents are able to see not just academic grades but also the student's participation and achievement in different school programmes as well as a description of the child's personal qualities, such as responsibility, teamwork and perseverance.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are making progress towards holistic education, but this remains a journey.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our students can discover their interests and develop their character and strengths through a range of CCAs and school programmes.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MOE encourages students to participate in CCAs, even if they do not represent their schools.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will strive towards this across schools, subject to limited school resources.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They are also given the flexibility to join various CCAs throughout their education journey, or take more than one CCA if they so wish, provided they can cope.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Outdoor Education (OE) is another platform that provides rich learning experiences outside the classroom for building Page: 28 resilience, tenacity and ruggedness in our youth.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Since 2014, we have set aside formal curriculum time in all primary and secondary schools for OE as part of physical education (PE) lessons.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: School camps are another way of immersing our students in authentic and often challenging situations, where they need to work in teams and learn to take responsibility for decisions they make.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These experiences develop a culture of self-reliance and mutual support with their peers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: On a recent camp visit, I met some Primary 5 students who were learning how to cook a simple meal outdoors with instant noodles.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For some of them, it was the first time they had ever lit a matchstick.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: On another occasion, I was told the story of a group of Secondary 1 students who boiled water in mess tins over an open fire to make hot chocolate.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They shared that it was the most delicious hot chocolate that they had ever tasted, simply because they made it.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I was heartened to see that even simple activities like these can help our children build a sense of independence and appreciation for daily comforts.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Small as these examples may be, they are meaningful and much needed experiences.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Today, our students participate in about two or three school cohort camps at upper primary and secondary levels.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Over the next few years, we will progressively rejuvenate and upgrade camp facilities at our MOE Outdoor Adventure Learning Centres.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will offer new camp programmes and raise the competencies of camp facilitators.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are also partnering MCCY to build the new OBS campus on Coney Island.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This camp provides a unique opportunity for students from different schools to collaborate and overcome challenges in the outdoors.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Their common experience will contribute towards building a stronger Singaporean identity, a point raised by Mr Seah Kian Peng.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Under the National Outdoor Adventure Education Master Plan, MOE will also continue to partner outdoor adventure service providers to offer varied programmes to our schools, both locally and overseas.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They have expertise that our schools can tap on.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Together with OBS and other partners, MOE is committed to raising the quality and quantity of our outdoor adventure learning programmes for our students.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: To date, many students have benefited from their OBS experience, including our Prime Minister, who shared on his Facebook page how OBS was a significant growing-up experience for him.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Michelle Chua is a Secondary 4 student from Jurongville Secondary School who also had a memorable OBS experience in Pulau Ubin.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Page: 29 She recounted how her team lost their way on the second day of a three-day land-trekking expedition.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This set the team back by several hours, probably delaying their dinner time.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Despite the hunger and exhaustion, the group of students encouraged one another and sang in unison to motivate one another on the way back.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: That night, when they arrived back at camp, they were last among all the teams.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But they kept their spirits high and were unfazed by this setback.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The next day, with better planning and teamwork to navigate and pace their trek, they came in first.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The panel will be chaired by Dr Tan Lai Yong, who is well-regarded for his work with the youths and community and who is currently Director for Outreach and Community Engagement at the College of Alice and Peter Tan at the National University of Singapore (NUS).

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The second, and a very key part of the shift that we want to achieve, is to reduce excessive focus on academic results.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ms Denise Phua, Dr Intan Mokhtar and Mr Seah Kian Peng spoke on this, especially with regard to the PSLE.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Today, there is a deeply ingrained mindset that the PSLE is a very high-stakes exam.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Many perceive that a child's PSLE T-score at the age of 12 determines his or her success and pathway in life.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But we know that this is not true, from the many stories of many who have done well in life despite not having done so well in PSLE.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: What we observe is that a student's PSLE indicates the progress that a child has made in his or her learning in primary school, but it does not cast in stone what he or she can achieve in the future, in life.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And as a parent, I can empathise with that.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is easy to get fixated on what is measurable.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We put a score on something and that makes it easy for us to compare with one another.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But what is measurable, sometimes, may not be what is most important in the long run.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Chasing after that last point in an exam could come at a cost to other aspects of our children's overall development, especially at a young age: too many anxious late nights, too much tuition and too little quality time for family and friends, for play and for exploration.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin raised concerns that the amount of homework that our children have is excessive.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Given appropriately, homework reinforces students' learning, contributes to their progress and cultivates a healthy disposition towards learning.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, I agree that more is not always better, and the amount of homework has to be calibrated appropriately.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: All our schools have put in place a homework policy and mechanisms to regulate, monitor and coordinate homework across departments and subjects.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: People often draw comparisons between education and botany.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I am not much of a gardener, but I did plant some green beans for a school project when I was a small boy.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I remember waking up each morning, impatiently monitoring my glass jar day after day, waiting for the first shoot to sprout.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I soon realised that over-watering my seedlings did not make them grow any faster.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I believe our children, like young seedlings, ought to have time and space to breathe, learn and dream.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Page: 30 So, there is a need to reduce this over-emphasis on academic results.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have made several steps in this direction over the last few years.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For example, in 2012, we stopped naming the top PSLE scorers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Today, we celebrate students' performance in all domains, across both academic and non-academic areas.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But we can do more to change mind-sets and culture.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Prime Minster had announced in 2013 that we would review the PSLE scoring system.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The main issue to address is that the way we currently score PSLE is too precise and differentiates our students more finely than necessary.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: A student may score one point more than his friend at PSLE, but educationally, that one point does not mean that he is better prepared for secondary school than his friend.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It also does not mean that he is very much smarter or will grow up to be more capable or lead a more successful or fulfilling life.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We should therefore, in time, move away from such fine distinctions, which are not meaningful, especially at that young age.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The way that the T-score is calculated may have also created unhealthy competition among our young children.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Because it is calculated based on how students do relative to one another, students may feel the pressure to do better than their peers rather than help one another out to learn.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This runs counter to the values we want to inculcate in our children.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We can find a better balance between encouraging our students to study hard and get good results, and making them overly-competitive and anxious about outdoing one another.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our over-arching objective in the primary school years is to build strong foundations for learning in our children.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: After studying the issues carefully, we propose to make a few changes to the PSLE scoring system.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Some broad level of differentiation is still needed to guide students to academic programmes that best suit their interests and strengths.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is more educationally meaningful than assessing a student's performance relative to his peers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It will still be a fair and transparent system based on academic merit.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In doing so, students can consider factors, such as the school's distinctive programmes, CCAs, and partnerships with the community and industry, and better match these factors with their interests.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The current PSLE system is well-established and we must be fully ready before moving to the new system.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: So, we will take the next few years to work through these changes carefully.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have already begun our journey of evolving our school landscape.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We want to give all schools time to develop Page: 31 their distinctive strengths and niche programmes towards the vision of every school a good school.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Meanwhile, we will need to develop and test the new PSLE scoring and posting systems thoroughly.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Over the next few months, MOE will be working closely with our school leaders and educators on the proposed changes.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
