text: We will subsequently also engage parents and members of the public on these changes and provide an update at the COS debate in 2017.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The third part of this paradigm shift is to offer more opportunities for different expressions of merit and achievements, across all schools.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Academic merit continues to be important in secondary school posting, because our primary school students should be matched to secondary schools that would be a good fit for their aptitudes.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, there is scope for greater flexibility in how we recognise different forms of merit and achievements in the overall Secondary 1 posting system.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We want to encourage students and parents to choose schools carefully, so that they can select a school which can best nurture their interests and strengths.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The DSA scheme was introduced back in 2004 for this very purpose.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The intent of DSA is to open up opportunities for students to be recognised for a range of achievements and talents when seeking admission into secondary school.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It also allows some flexibility on the school's part to admit students with specific aptitudes, so that the distinctive programmes offered by the school benefit the right profile of students.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I recently visited Admiralty Secondary School and met a Secondary 3 boy.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: His name is Jun Heng; he is somewhat of a shy and quiet boy.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, behind his soft-spoken demeanour, I discovered a bright young man full of passion for programming and robotics.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: There is a sparkle in his eyes when he speaks about robotics.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Jun Heng has had an interest in robotics since he joined his primary school's robotics club.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: He was so eager to pursue this further in secondary school that he applied through DSA to join Admiralty Secondary School, which has a well-known robotics enterprise programme and won many national and international competitions.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: When I asked him why he likes robotics so much, he said, quite simply to me, "Because there are no limits to what you can do".

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: That is what inspired me about Jun Heng's story.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This young man makes his choices and takes concrete steps towards his dreams with conviction.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I am very glad that he chose a school that is a great fit for him and I wish him all the very best.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: There are many more students like Jun Heng who begin to discover their passions early, through their CCAs or activities.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These can be further nurtured in secondary school.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: With a more diverse and vibrant secondary school landscape, we want to enable more students to benefit from the DSA scheme and tap on the range of programmes our schools offer.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will complement the changes to the PSLE system.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Learning from more than a decade of implementing DSA, we know that many students have benefited from this opportunity.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: At the same time, there is some unevenness in how different schools select their DSA students.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is timely, therefore, to take a step back and see how to realign the implementation of this scheme with its original policy intent.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: First, we would like to expand opportunities in more secondary schools for students with specific aptitudes and talents to enter a school with distinctive programmes via DSA.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will provide students with more options when selecting a school that can best nurture their interests and talents.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Second, we would sharpen the focus of DSA to better recognise talents and achievements in specific domains, rather than general academic ability that can be demonstrated through the PSLE.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MOE will consider the views on DSA shared by Ms Denise Phua and Dr Intan, and we will share more details about the DSA review in due course.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In sum, with changes to the PSLE scoring system, DSA and a more variegated secondary school landscape, we will create more opportunities and choices for students at the Secondary 1 posting juncture.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I want to encourage all our students to consider carefully which secondary schools offer education pathways and opportunities that are best suited for you, based on your specific aptitudes and aspirations.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Get to know your schools better, beyond their cut-off points.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: If you do not quite know what you want to do yet or are passionate about, that is okay, too.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Whichever school you choose to go, give yourself the time and space to explore different domains and learn new things.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MOE and our educators will be there to support you.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: At the same time, we are committed to investing in all schools and providing the resources to develop our students holistically and fully.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Png Eng Huat and Mr Dennis Tan asked about how we fund our schools equitably.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MOE resources schools based on the needs of students, programmes offered by the schools and the enrolment of the schools.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Over the years, we have significantly increased funding for education across all levels and schools.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In fact, where we could, within our limited resources, we have been more generous in allocating more for our mainstream schools.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Besides funding, we also ensure that our schools are adequately resourced with teachers to meet the needs of our students.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We decided more than a decade ago to grow the teaching Page: 33 workforce.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh enquired if we could reduce the class sizes in mainstream schools to the levels in OECD countries.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Rather than reducing class sizes across the board, we adopt the approach to deploy resources in a much more targeted way, to support areas of greater educational need.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This allows our schools to implement appropriate intervention strategies and give individual attention to low-progress students and students with special learning needs.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We think this is a better and more inclusive approach to deploy the limited resources that we have.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Furthermore, it is not conclusive that smaller class sizes improve student outcomes on a system-wide basis.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In fact, studies show that teacher quality matters much more.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: While we do not rule out further improvements in class sizes, we must balance this carefully with what is sustainable, and not risk compromising the quality of teachers we recruit.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We also want to help students to be posted to schools that can cater to their learning needs and interests.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I spoke about the changes to the Secondary 1 posting and school landscape earlier, which will provide more choices and opportunities for posting.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For younger students in primary schools, we recognise that the distance between home and school is also an important consideration for school choices and posting.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked if MOE could review the current Primary 1 (P1) registration framework to give more priority to students living near primary schools.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The P1 registration framework carefully balances various factors and is not limited to just home-school distance.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Other factors include elder siblings, community involvement and the schools' ties with their stakeholders.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Nevertheless, I would like to assure Mr Lim Biow Chuan that MOE will continue to ensure sufficient school places on a regional basis, so that our young children will not have to travel far to primary school.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In addition, MOE will also promote OE to nurture resilience, ruggedness and tenacity in our students.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Page: 34 Every child is like a seedling.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We should not be overly anxious and rush their growth, as pulling young seedlings harms them instead.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Nor should we over-shelter them, or they will become delicate flowers that are unable to weather the storms of life.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have to understand and balance the different needs of each seedling and nurture them with care.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: With adequate sunlight, water and space, our children can freely grow into sturdy trees that are firmly rooted.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We must nurture future generations of Singaporeans who are not only successful, but also have a sense of belonging, national identity and care for fellow citizens.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Therefore, we will continue to emphasise character education in our schools in order to cultivate the right values in our students from a young age.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These outcomes may not be easily measured, but they last through life and help our children to be better-prepared for the future.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We can then nurture a strong "Singapore Heartbeat", united towards our common vision.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: (In English): Mdm Chair, let me now speak about an inclusive education system.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We must ensure that every Singaporean can find their own pathway to success and be part of the nation's progress, regardless of their starting points and background.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is the essence of a united Singapore Heartbeat that I spoke about in my maiden speech.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: While we cannot ensure equal outcomes, we must provide children equal access to opportunities in all our schools.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ms Denise Phua and Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked for an update on what MOE is doing further to level the playing field for students from disadvantaged backgrounds and provide dedicated support to those who are academically weaker.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Children enter our schools with different starting points, abilities and learning needs.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We must continue to do our utmost to provide pathways for every child.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Beyond Primary 2, low-progress students continue to be supported through other programmes all the way to secondary school.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These Specialised Schools adopt a whole-school approach and customise their curriculum and pedagogy to the learning needs of their students.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Third, and very importantly, we resource schools and train teachers to support our low-progress learners.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Learning Support Programmes that I mentioned earlier are centrally-designed and taught by teachers who are specially trained to engage low-progress learners and be able to address not just their academic needs but their socio-emotional needs effectively.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our goal is not just to help them level up in their studies, but also to develop their self-confidence and self- Page: 35 esteem.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As I have explained, we already have differentiated and dedicated support for low-progress learners, including those from needy families.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our context and approach are quite different from many other countries.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are able to centrally train and deploy teachers, being a small country.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: So, I am proud to say that we already have a national corps of well-trained teachers for all students.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Students with financial needs should benefit from a quality education, regardless of their family's circumstances.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Muhamad Faisal Abdul Manap asked about the extension of assistance schemes, awards and funds.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MOE heavily subsidises the cost of education for all Singaporean students in our schools.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Many Members, including Mr Zainal Sapari and Dr Lim Wee Kiak, have asked about what more we can do in early childhood to provide every child with a strong start.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will give more details on MOE's efforts in this area.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: He will provide an update on how we are enhancing support for children with special educational needs.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is an issue that Ms Denise Phua, Ms Chia Yong Yong and Mr Zainal Sapari spoke passionately about just now.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I earlier used the metaphors of flowers and seedlings.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Chinese proverb "十年树木，百年树人" compares the task of nurturing people to growing trees – it takes 10 years to grow trees, but 100 to nurture people.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Education is a far more complex and arduous task than growing trees; nevertheless, we can extract useful insights.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As gardeners, we must tend our seedlings with great skill, care and love by ensuring that the plant has sufficient, but not overly harsh sunlight, and watering the plant based on how much the soil can take.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: More importantly, as the seedlings grow and take root, we should hold back and give them enough space and freedom to flourish.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We must not over-shelter them or suffocate them with too much watering and over-fertilising, but allow them to grow upright, strong and sturdy and resilient to any storms.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Today, I fear we are overcrowding our young ones with a narrow focus on academics.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: While we have their best interests at heart, too much of one thing impedes, rather than supports, overall growth.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I believe the changes in the PSLE system, the DSA review and the OE programmes are critical to preparing our children for the future.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These changes will contribute to reducing the emphasis on exam results and give more time and opportunities for every student to develop as a well-rounded individual.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, there is no easy solution, no silver bullet, to the issues of stress and competition that Members raised.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I started out saying that education is both a personal journey as well as a societal concern.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Hence, while MOE can change policies and structures, ultimately, this is a personal journey for Page: 36 every child, parent and family.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is a partnership among MOE, educators, students, parents and even employers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Collectively, our choices will determine whether we can succeed in making this paradigm shift to free up time and space for holistic education.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Let us help our children to make good use of their time to branch out to explore other interests and passions and to pursue what they want to do in life.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Let us help them to make good choices about their educational and career pathways based on their aptitudes and aspirations.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Let us help them to be ready for the future.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This, indeed, will be the best gift that we can present to our next generation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To make this a reality, some children need more help.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We cannot treat every child in exactly the same manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Some children have special needs, some have learning difficulties and others come from less-privileged backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To achieve equality of opportunity and bring out the best in all of them, we need to treat each child differently.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: More needs to be done for certain groups of students who need our attention the most.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This will appear as an unequal distribution of time, effort and resources.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: An inclusive education system has to start in the child's early years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is when children develop literacy, numeracy, socio-emotional skills and a sense of curiosity and wonder.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But we need to recognise that we should not be over-preparing our children for primary school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar has pointed out that we have already achieved almost universal access to preschool.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We recognise that having some parental choice and involvement in the type of experience a child has at preschool is important.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our current system allows for this, and compulsory education for preschool may not be the best way forward.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Nevertheless, the Government will continue to explore ways to provide every child the opportunity to benefit from a structured preschool experience.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Mr Zainal Sapari asked about early childhood education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have and will continue to invest substantial resources in improving preschool education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The first batch of MK children is now in Primary 1, and parents have shared that their children have the confidence and social skills to adapt well to primary school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOE will continue to engage partners and stakeholders in the early childhood education sector to see how we can best use the lessons learned from the MK programme to help all children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Since 2014, we have been sharing good teaching and learning practices at various platforms, including the annual MOE Mother Tongue Language Symposium and the annual Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) Early Childhood conference.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: From this year, we will be sharing teaching and learning resources we call "Big Books".

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They are quite large books, for English and Mother Tongue languages, large in font and format, not necessarily very thick.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These "Big Books" have been piloted at our MKs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The teachers can use these "Big Books" as a structured approach towards language-learning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This will help more preschool Page: 37 children to speak and read in English and their Mother Tongues with confidence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This programme is especially important if you come from a background or a family that does not have English as a common language at home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: English literacy becomes a foundation for studying a wide variety of other subjects – Science and Mathematics, for example, for assessing knowledge on your own in a library and for achieving the sort of self-directed learning that you need to access knowledge on the Internet.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, the FLAiR programme is available as an additional support for all children who need it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We want to replicate and extend FLAiR's success by increasing the number of anchor operator-run preschool centres offering FLAiR, and it has now been made available to not-for-profit centres.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I agree with Ms Denise Phua about the need to level the playing field for all children, regardless of their backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We ensure that education is heavily subsidised for all students at all levels, and we provide additional financial assistance for needy students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The provision of technology can also be a social leveller.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We give all our schools the resources to provide their students, including the underprivileged ones, with access to computing devices for learning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The online learning space that Ms Denise Phua spoke about, we will take this a step further by giving all students access to self-paced learning anytime and anywhere.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This also allows teachers to design lessons and upload them and share work among students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This will also make possible the provision of third-party applications and education ware, including open-source applications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These can be developed separately, to be integrated for use by both teachers and students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui will be pleased to note that we also guide our students to be responsible and safe online.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: All our schools teach cyber wellness and also appoint students as "Cyber Wellness Student Ambassadors" to help guide their fellow students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our ITE, polytechnics and autonomous universities also teach cyber wellness in a number of ways, including guidelines, compulsory modules, orientation camps and online platforms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: During and after school hours, we aim to provide a supportive environment for all children, especially those from less-privileged backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOE has supported the establishment of these school-based Student Care Centres (SCCs) that provide after-school care, supervision and development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Page: 38 Promoting health is another way we can provide support for our students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Equipping children with social and emotional competencies help to increase their mental well-being, reduce risky behaviours and improve academic outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Kok Heung Leun will be pleased to know that social and emotional competencies have been included in the school curriculum a decade ago and are also incorporated with the revised CCE curriculum.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Students go through the process of acquiring the skills to recognise and manage emotions, develop care and concern for others, make responsible decisions, establish positive relationships and handle challenging situations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I would also like to reassure Mr Kok that teachers do use stories of loss, stories of managing change in family circumstances, from Literature as well as from the media to reinforce these lessons and, particularly, to highlight the need for resilience and to develop the mental and social skills in order for the children to have resilience.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These values and socio-emotional competencies are reinforced during CCAs and camps.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The CCE curriculum also aims to inculcate other 21st century competencies, such as civic literacy and critical thinking.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Many teachers whom I have met feel that this is a central part of their duty.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They have a moral obligation to not just be educators but also provide a degree of care and social support for the students they are in charge of looking after.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Away from the public eye, there are many circumstances that I have come across in my previous professional life where it was the teacher who demonstrated a very deep understanding of some of the traumas that an underprivileged or vulnerable child may go through and was able to support both the child as well as the family that they were in touch with.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: All teachers are equipped with the skills and knowledge to help our students develop character and the kind of competencies that Mr Kok spoke about.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They have to take a CCE module during their pre-service training, which also includes opportunities for them to engage in dialogue with experienced CCE teachers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In addition, all teachers have to take on Service Learning Projects to prepare them to conduct VIA programmes in schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These two modules, these two ideas of a CCE module and Service Learning Project, in the teacher training process informs us on how we map some of our expectations of behaviours and values that we have of our students to the process that the teachers undergo in their training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, what we expect in terms of values and behaviours for our students inside our curriculum and in our schools are expressed through the expectations we have of our trainee teachers while they are being trained to be teachers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There is a very tight link between the two.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To address Mr Png Eng Huat's concerns, these VIA programmes are central to our aim of developing a strong civic consciousness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Students learn to take responsibility for their own spaces in class and at home at the primary school level, before progressing to initiating collective action among their peers to improve the lives of others in school and the community at the secondary school level and beyond.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This year, we have reinforced being responsible for the community in a very tangible and physical way.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: All primary school students play a part in cleaning their schools every day − learning good habits, good values, respecting their school environment and the people who work to keep Page: 39 their schools clean.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I would, first, like to assure Dr Intan Mokhtar that the majority of these children, who have relatively mild special educational needs, are already in mainstream schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We, at MOE, and many of their families believe that these children can cope with the rigours of a mainstream curriculum once they are given a little extra support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOE will continue to recruit more going forward.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We do wish to recruit more going forward and extend the availability of this service.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But they are doing an important and challenging job.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have to recruit the right people with the right disposition and skills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have invested heavily in training both teachers and AEDs(LBS).

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As Ms Chia Yong Yong has pointed out, we give our schools the flexibility to source specific programmes to meet local specific needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But these school-based programmes merely supplement the structured training already provided at NIE, our key training partner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: All teachers, during their pre-service training, are equipped with an awareness of special educational needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: AEDs(LBS) undergo the full-time pre-service Diploma in Special Education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Advanced Diploma in Special Education is also available to them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We work with the Dyslexia Association of Singapore and the Autism Resource Centre to provide these AEDs(LBS) staff with in-service training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As we are committed to training teachers and the allied educators well, we will continue to review the structured training available to them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This helps students with dyslexia to overcome their core difficulties in reading and spelling.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As part of the programme, we have also developed resources to enable parents to help their children at home to overcome the challenge of dyslexia.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: More students with special educational needs are entering our IHLs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Rather than be concerned about the average disbursements or a particular target, what is important is that these students have access to resources matched to their needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Some students need a very small intervention, such as a ramp or a mechanical keyboard, whereas other students need a very wide series of both physical as well as process interventions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, the average may not be very meaningful.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For the smaller group of students with more severe special educational needs, we believe that they are better catered for in Special Education (SPED) schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These schools are provided substantial funding by MOE – significantly more than the mainstream schools – which goes towards paying specialised staff and providing more intensive support for their students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have worked closely with SPED schools to provide a quality education and to help prepare the children for life after school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To cite just one example, we have piloted the School-to-Work Page: 40 Transition Programme in five SPED schools with MSF and SGEnable so that more students can be gainfully employed upon graduation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We identify these students' interests and strengths and put in place structured internships and customised training pathways, with support from job coaches in various organisations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Most of the participants from the first cohort are now successfully employed in a wide range of industries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The School-to-Work programme will be made available to more SPED schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOE is working with interested schools to put in place new processes to enable them to identify and support their students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As we look to improve the transition from school to work, a consistent challenge is the mindset of employers and co-workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This will take time to change and I urge all Singaporeans to keep an open mind, to offer these students and the adults they grow into every chance to be part of our society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Denise Phua suggested co-locating SPED schools and mainstream schools to promote inclusivity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We need a range of inclusive practices to cater to a range of different needs and allow for meaningful interaction and integration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our satellite partnership model includes this range of practices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Some SPED schools practise "social integration" with their mainstream partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Others, like Pathlight School, allow their students to join their mainstream peers in class.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Canossian School practises "full inclusion" and its students already join in mainstream classes for all academic and non-academic activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In addressing Mr Zainal Sapari's concerns regarding SPED schools, I would like to point out that the majority of SPED schools – 13 out of the 20 schools – charge around $10 to $20 per month.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is comparable to fees at Government schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The remaining seven SPED schools charge higher fees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is because they cater to students with multiple disabilities and challenges, who have a greater need for additional educational and therapy support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Nonetheless, their fees are still significantly lower than private SPED schools or international schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In addition, MOE provides help for needy families through the SPED Financial Assistance Scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These schools also offer fee subsidies for eligible students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will continue to work with SPED schools to improve their affordability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Over the years, we have been upgrading school premises, setting up new schools and expanding existing ones to allow more students to access special education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In the past few years, we have built a new campus for Delta Senior School, expanded Metta School and created additional classrooms for Pathlight School.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: More than physical capacity, skilled, committed and passionate staff are at the heart of our efforts to support children in SPED schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Just last year, we made available more funds for SPED schools to increase the salaries of teachers, allied professionals and other staff.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is not only to help schools attract and retain personnel, but also to recognise the crucial and challenging work they do every day.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Speaking to everybody in all the schools − the members of the board, the education and therapy staff, the nurse who mans the medical bay − you get a very pervasive sense of mission, purpose, pride and professionalism.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They explain how much they are devoted to this calling that they have, the work that they do and the students that they care for.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But from the outside, it does not look so much like just a job or the professional pride in their job; it looks like love.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They love the institutions that they have supported and worked for, raised funds for and volunteered for.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There are problems with the physicality of their work, but it does not stop them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They love what they do and they love their Page: 41 students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Over the years, they have built up a deep expertise in catering to specific disability types.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: If implemented effectively, it will sustain Singapore's competitive advantage and help our people get good jobs and have fulfilling careers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is especially critical at a time when many workers have to keep pace with rapid technological changes whilst others, affected by economic restructuring, have to be reskilled, possibly multiple times, throughout their working life.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: SkillsFuture can provide that lifeline for Singaporeans to ride the waves of change, rather than be dragged down and crushed by disruptive forces in the marketplace.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There must be clear linkages from training courses, to skills, to jobs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And I repeat: there must be clear linkages from training courses, to skills, to jobs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Equally important is the information on industry growth clusters where vacancies exist and where future jobs will flourish.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There should be a simple tool to help people narrow down their options, to focus their efforts.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For a segment of the less-educated older Singaporeans who will have difficulty going online to search for courses, we must have an alternative ready for them.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To fully leverage SkillsFuture, we should start with better career guidance for school leavers to choose their future vocation well, so that they are well-guided in their choice of post-secondary education.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should learn from the best practices in Switzerland where about two-thirds of 15- to 16-year-old students leave school to start their vocational training.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Before leaving school, students should have the opportunity to have "look-see" experiences at vocations that may interest them, carried out in a very systematic way, whether they are curious about being a doctor, a chef or a computer programmer.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Companies and trade associations should work with MOE to conduct "open house" exercises to provide insights to jobs, working environments and career prospects in their industry.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Page: 42 Madam, I was happy to hear Acting Minister Ng Chee Meng speaking about nurturing interests and passion in students in his speech.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I have received many appeals from young people who are disappointed that they have missed the entrance marks to the study of their choice despite a very clear interest and passion for their area of study.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Therefore, I would like to appeal that IHLs consider providing places to prospective students who have demonstrated a passion for the field of study they are applying for, in addition to being assessed purely on academic results.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Presently, the most urgent need for SkillsFuture is to really help the retrenched professionals find their feet, rebuild confidence, guide them to acquire new skills and, more importantly, find ways to get employers on board to provide job opportunities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There must be significantly more effort invested on "place and train".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The connection between training and employability must be more direct and stronger, so as to provide a line of sight between the efforts that one puts into retraining and the hope for re-employment.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: SkillsFuture will only succeed with careful planning and coordination among all key stakeholders – individuals, employers and the Government − to ensure the right set of outcomes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Government's active involvement should in no way diminish the employers' critical role in training and developing their employees.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I would like to ask the Acting Minister how companies are complementing the efforts of SkillsFuture to develop their staff, including the provision of annual leave.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: At the same time, we also need to develop a system to ensure that the courses eligible for SkillsFuture credits are of acceptable quality.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: While SkillsFuture caters mainly to working adults who want to upgrade their skills so that they are still relevant in the job market, it also caters to elderly Singaporeans who want to upgrade themselves in their golden years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, it would be good if the course directory of SkillsFuture can include a section that consolidates courses which are more suitable for retired adults.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If there is no age limit, could Singaporeans who have passed on transfer their SkillsFuture credits to their loved ones?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For SkillsFuture to be inclusive, I hope that the Workforce Development Agency (WDA) and other Government agencies could devote some time developing suitable courses for persons with disability or make provisions for some of the existing courses to be friendly for persons with disability to attend.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If this suggestion is acceptable to the Acting Minister, the SkillsFuture course directory could also include a section dedicated to persons with disability to reflect the focus in this area.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: UniSIM has a large enrolment of working adults and is involved in the provision of SkillsFuture courses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As the Minister for Finance has emphasised, providing good jobs is a priority.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is also important to ensure that workers with the right skills are available to take such jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: A prolonged shortage of workers with the requisite skills will, ultimately, put the job creation process under intense pressure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If the supply of workers with the right skill sets is not forthcoming, job creation will have to adjust to the realities of labour supply.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: For decades, our labour market policy had been able to address this challenge, supported by intricate planning from MOE.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: However, technological disruption and increasingly intense global economic competition threaten to catch us unprepared.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is not easy to predict the impact of SkillsFuture on individual organisations, including education institutions like mine.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Will the emphasis on acquiring skills lead to a reduction of emphasis on achieving qualifications?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Regardless of whether it does, what will happen to institutions which do not promote skills-based learning?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Some will be caught unprepared, while others will be much more prepared and come out well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Individuals will not be spared from the consequences of being caught unprepared.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But how does one prepare for SkillsFuture and what does it mean to be prepared?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: To begin with, I think we should look at SkillsFuture as a journey, one in which we must be prepared for the long haul, pace ourselves and not deplete our resources, including our enthusiasm, too quickly, and ensure we reach the destination that matches our individual objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Learning journeys for working adults often take place against a backdrop of individual and family sacrifices, unlike full-time students with neither dependants nor work responsibilities, the most mundane aspects present challenges for adult learners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This can range from what time they should leave work to navigate rush-hour traffic in order not to be late for lectures, to whether family time or home work should take priority over a weekend.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Working adults who take night classes experience such difficulties more than others, without any recognition and little understanding of their circumstances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Acquiring skills can also be accompanied by dirt and grime.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The providers of Earn and Learn placements reveal the reality of the job environment without flashy trappings, comfortable surroundings and swanky privileges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: They end up with few or no takers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Artificially jazzing up everything just to attract interest risks misrepresenting the facts about what lies ahead for SkillsFuture aspirants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The mindset with which both individuals and organisations embrace their SkillsFuture journey is, therefore, important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, one of the most important hurdles I foresee is the way Page: 44 SkillsFuture aspirants perceive themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This issue may have an impact on how deep the effort goes in effecting real change in our workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has done its part, but how will it sustain its effort for the long term without getting caught up in superficial indicators of performance?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: However, this has to be balanced against an overly heavy focus on chasing KPIs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We should be careful not to lose sight of the length of the SkillsFuture journey and the rigours to be endured by those who embark upon it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: How do we balance these two − the need for accountability and the desire to allow each individual enough room to learn at a pace to fit their needs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, how do we balance the long-term goals with the short-term need for accountability?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Acquiring skills on the job is quite different from acquiring knowledge in the classroom.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In classroom-based learning, experimentation and trial-and-error are positively encouraged.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: There is little doubt that employers would want their workers to deepen their skills on the job.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, while both experimentation and trial-and-error are inevitable in a workplace setting, they are meant to be incidental.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Performing the task at hand correctly each time is the priority in a workplace setting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Even as the physical boundaries of the classroom become blurred, such distinctions would have to be appreciated in order for stakeholders to keep faith in one another and remain committed to the SkillsFuture journey.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: SkillsFuture courses are very diverse, from Aerospace to Domestic Cleaning, Marine and Port Services to Tourism.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: I am interested to know what are the checks and mechanisms in place to maintain consistent standards and encourage providers to keep their content updated and relevant.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: What are also some measures that will be put in place to prevent potential abuse of the schemes by the vendors?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Would the Ministry also share how often audits will be conducted on training providers and their companies?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: I also tried checking up the various types of approved courses on the website and it is actually not quite friendly.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: In addition, can there also be a platform for interested learners to exchange information and feedback about the courses with past participants and the vendors?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: As we continue to expand and deepen SkillsFuture, I hope we will continue to extend reasonable accommodation to seniors and persons with disabilities to enable them to secure job opportunities and attain career progression.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: In addition, I would like to bring to the attention of the House a group of special students.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: They have disabilities, and are mostly attending SPED schools.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: This group of students will finish school at a much later age than their peers.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It is a significant commitment in Singapore's next phase of people development.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The success of SkillsFuture lies in building a culture of lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Each individual must have an intrinsic motivation to identify his areas of interests and pursue them to achieve deeper skills mastery.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: So, I was heartened by the introduction of the SkillsFuture Credit earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: This will empower everyone to chart and embark upon his or her own lifelong learning journey.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I have received several initial positive feedback on the SkillsFuture Credit from residents and others.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Some are still thinking about how they should use their credits, but a few others have already started to explore courses that they would not have had taken otherwise.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: This, I think, is a good development, as it spurs individuals to start thinking about their own learning journeys.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Last month, I opened an exhibition by the first batch of SkillsFuture students who completed a course in Digital Photography Technology and Techniques at UniSIM.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The students came from all walks of life.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: There was a freelance photographer who said that the course has enhanced his skills.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Another student, who is a corporate trainer, told me that with better photography skills, he could make his teaching materials more interesting.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I have requests from senior citizens to transfer their SkillsFuture credits into their MediSave or their children's SkillsFuture account, as they could not find a suitable course.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Some said that they are already in their 70s or 80s; what more can they learn or should they learn?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: To be fully effective, the list of courses eligible for the SkillsFuture Credit should cater to a broader range of interests.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: On that note, I would like to ask MOE what are the additional or new types of SkillsFuture courses that will be open for Singaporeans, including seniors, because only then can we truly promote lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister on the uptake of this programme thus far, including the profile of Singaporeans who have utilised their SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Council for Private Education (CPE), which is responsible for regulating our private education sector, has the challenging task of ensuring the quality of these schools.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Page: 46 Many more courses in diverse fields will be offered under SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If CPE's experience can be used as a benchmark, it will be challenging to "patrol" so many programmes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we ensure that prospective students are enrolling in reliable and relevant programmes?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The ones who know what they want to do already have a particular field and specific courses in mind.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, they might not be sure what progression the course will lead to.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Then there are those who are overwhelmed by the sheer number of courses, of which some can be rather similar-sounding.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This group may end up spending their SkillsFuture credits randomly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The third group might not have the information technology (IT) literacy skills to trawl through the directory of courses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our Singaporeans might need guidance to spend the credit wisely.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In an Amazon-style course curation system, users will be able to get course suggestions based on their training preferences and peer reviews.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also ensures that course providers constantly upgrade and innovate to cater to industry's and users' demand.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry create platforms for peer reviews to be shared publicly to differentiate the quality of courses and guide Singaporeans better?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can the Ministry help Singaporeans to navigate the training terrain better?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For workers to deep-skill and traverse industries, they can be provided with sectoral-based pathways and skills ladders linked to training courses in the SkillsFuture directory.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These skills and competencies should also be mapped to economic and manpower needs to optimise manpower usage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Sectoral Tripartite Committees have been developing their sectoral manpower plans (SMPs) to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Do they seek to feature the courses in the said directory?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: SkillsFuture should also be about providing workers with options to secure their future and livelihood.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, many residents questioned why Class 3 Driving Licence is not included even though it can lead to many driving-based jobs or enhance their employability?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To many lower-income workers, it secures livelihoods in the event of retrenchment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In comparison, for example, floral arrangement, which is in the course directory, is interesting and can be a useful skill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But it might not lead to the immediate broader array of opportunities from a Class 3 driving licence.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The stepping up of the Professional Conversion Programmes (PCP) will also help more Singaporeans adapt, grow their skills and find a new career path.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I have also received feedback that the sheer number and wide-ranging choices can be overwhelming for an individual to choose from.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some may just jump into the training bandwagon and sign on courses without giving adequate thought about the areas they really need to invest in.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Others may follow in the footsteps of their friends or peers or succumb to the persuasions of advertisements.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To enhance their decision making, I would like to propose that individuals be allowed to use their SkillsFuture Credit to attend sessions conducted by professional life coaches.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Typically, life coaching sessions allow attendees to set clear goals, assess their current realities, run through options and determine the next best step forward.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The concept of life coaching is still quite new in Singapore, but it is gaining popularity among working adults.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry consider including life coaching under the SkillsFuture credit course directory?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Coaching format can also be in a group setting besides the usual one-to-one sessions.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With SkillsFuture, we want to empower our workers with skills mastery and inculcate a lifelong learning attitude.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through a life coach, I believe that workers can do constant checks and reviews on their skills gaps, career goals and pathways of growth.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a bold new area but also a pre-emptive effort to prepare our workers to be in control of the career of their life and to be future-ready, instead of seeking help only when a problem arises or when they get retrenched.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I urge the Ministry to consider trying this unexplored area to help our workers take ownership of their careers and personal growth, to be fully aware of what their goals and aspirations are, and have the right drive and motivation to move towards realising them.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Students, and their parents, are naturally anxious about their future.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We know that some students feel pressured to consider popular jobs or pathways that may actually not be suited to their strengths.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Some may not know what is available and others may simply want a second opinion.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, they look to the experts, or ECG counsellors, for assistance.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: ECG counsellors are vested with heavy responsibility, and yet they are only human.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Already, it is no easy job to have at one's fingertips knowledge about the education system.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: It is harder still to imagine that ECG counsellors would have come into their role with knowledge about all kinds of jobs.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: There are new jobs in emerging fields, and existing jobs are constantly evolving.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Even industry experts find it challenging to predict what jobs will continue to exist, how Page: 48 they will change, how pay levels will evolve, and the whims of demand and supply.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: When I was a young boy, my ambition was to be a teacher.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I conducted lessons for my two younger brothers and made them do homework.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: However, I do not think I did so then because I had a lofty desire to nurture the younger generation, probably more to lord over my siblings.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Looking back, I had wanted to be a teacher then simply because it was the only job I knew.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: As a child or even teenager, our exposure was limited.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: That is where ECG counsellors help to fill the gap.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Seah Kian Peng, you have two cuts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: In the latest international rankings, we are placed higher than Yale.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: That partly comes from the willingness of our universities to attract overseas students and academics of calibre.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: This is part of our national psyche – we are an international island open to trade and global talent.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: However, we are a nation, first and foremost, a home for our people and a place where our children need to find their own footing, voice and identity.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: In all of this, our places of higher education play a crucial role.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: On the supply side, it could be that the pool of Singapore Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) students applying for an academic position locally is very small.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: It could be that many already have offers from the international job market and the 11 universities that are ranked higher than us.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: It could be that they are paid so much overseas that they prefer to teach elsewhere than in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: It could be; but I do not think so.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: The Minister has visited many IHLs, both in Singapore and abroad.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Does he think this is proportionate in a national university?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Second, I would like to ask what is the percentage of local professors in national universities in the US, the UK and Australia.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: I have raised this in Parliament in the past and was told that we do not have the numbers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: I would not be surprised if we still do not have them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: There is no way better to ensure that a man does not know something when his job depends on his not knowing it.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: I am not saying that we ought to hire Singaporeans only or even for any sort of nationalistic affirmative action policy, but merely to see if we can put local professors on a more equal footing.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Next, I wish to express my reservation about university rankings.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Rankings, be it Quacquarelli Symonds or Times Higher Education, may be construed as useful in many ways, and it is precisely these many ways of interpretations from different interest groups that I would like to ask the Minister what these agencies really measure and, for that matter, how they reflect our national priorities.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: The methodologies used to construct these rankings change, too, and we are not sure whether the climb upwards is because we are getting better or we are hitching a ride on changed methodologies or, worse, that we are restructuring ourselves so that we become more attractive to the people compiling these rankings.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Can the Minister tell us if the climb up the rankings factors in the KPIs of key administrators and what other considerations are taken into account?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: A few years ago, there were some consolidations in the private education industry sector.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Most parents would like their children to obtain a university degree.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Many graduates from the private universities may then be underemployed.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: At the same time, MOE could also encourage private universities to shift their focus and run courses geared towards lifelong learning under the Page: 50 SkillsFuture initiatives.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But let me, first, start by addressing the current worry that Ms Foo Mee Har has raised.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I chair the subcommittee on jobs and skills of CFE.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He is a journalist and I asked him what his readers expect out of the sub-committee.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And he said, "The economy is a bit sluggish, tell the students and the parents what to study, and after that what jobs to get.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You used to say it!" And when he said "you", he meant the Government.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Government used to say, study chemical engineering, biomed.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When I see young students today, some of them ask me the same question.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are two answers to this question, from two opposite, yet related, perspectives.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The first perspective, the first answer, is to understand the environment.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is very frustrating for a young person to graduate with a degree or diploma, step out into the workforce and find that there is no demand.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Something Mr Ang Wei Neng just mentioned, it happens in Korea, it happens in Taiwan.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must know how economic winds are blowing domestically, in the region, in the world and what is developing, what are the technological advancements.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: From this perspective, governments all have a duty to decipher all that is happening around us and signal to the people what are the areas to pursue.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second answer is to know the individual.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we can help every one of us discover our interests and aspirations, uncover innate talents and abilities and fulfil the potential of as many individuals as possible, that will become an enduring strength for the collective, for Singapore.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: From this perspective, what to learn is also a very personal enterprise; we must help each individual follow their respective rainbows.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will start with the first answer – understand the environment.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: While the global economy is sluggish, there are still opportunities.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is the case for every slowdown and recession.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are driven by the proliferation of the Internet of Things and our Smart Nation initiative.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We also need people to develop and operate public infrastructure, such as the new Changi Airport Terminals 4 and 5, plus new Mass Rapid Transit lines.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Government is ramping up the recruitment of engineers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) is building up its engineering corp, granting engineering scholarships.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We live in an exciting region with the markets around us presenting tremendous opportunities.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If Singapore-based companies can venture out to these markets and successfully tap into them, that will create many, many jobs for our people.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But it requires us to be able to go overseas, have boots on the ground and understand those markets.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har asked about helping PMEs who have lost their jobs to find new ones in such growth sectors.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is something that WDA has set out to do since it was formed in 2003.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And before we had PCP, we had SMCP, Place-and-train (PnT), Attach-and-Train (AnT) and several other schemes.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Minister Lim Swee Say will be speaking more on these during his Ministry's COS debate to help the retrenched and the misplaced to find employment again.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Now, the second answer, from the perspective of understanding the individual.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In this age of possibilities, we make room for a universe of purposes – encouraging our young people to find meaning in new and unimagined ways, such as new ways to deliver services, entertain the masses, power our industries, protect the environment, protect Singapore, or build machines to do things better and faster.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
